description: This case study records what happened in the United Kingdom during the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, the largest for over 20 years, and what the country should learn from it. Richard Horne and co-authors from the British Antarctic Survey, the British Geological Survey, the Civil Aviation Authority, Imperial College, Lancaster, Aberystwyth and other UK bodies published it in Royal Society Open Science in April 2026. The storm was a low-level G5 on the NOAA scale driven by five successive coronal mass ejections, and observed impacts were relatively minor. It exercised the UK Met Office forecasting system, communications and national preparedness and exposed weak points in power supplies, space traffic management, aviation, forecasting and data. Coverage is the United Kingdom. Format and access: an open access journal article; the publisher page asks for a browser check, so the abstract was read through OpenAlex. Licence: CC-BY-4.0; free. Caveats: a mild event tests procedures but not the reasonable worst case, and impacts are compiled from operators' reports. The authors make 14 recommendations to four government departments, useful for resilience and emergency response planning. Related catalogue records are the UK space weather reasonable worst-case scenarios and the US May 2024 GIC observations repository.
